title: Temporal associations of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological readiness is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of return to sport (RTS) and return to preinjury level (RTPre) of sport after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Functional outcomes are also relevant. However, the clinical significance of psychological readiness and functional outcomes may vary depending on the postoperative time point, and the association of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with RTS may be temporal. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the temporal association of psychological readiness and functional outcomes with RTS at different postoperative time points (≤6 months, <6-12 months, >12 months) after ACL reconstruction.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (PROSPERO CRD42025630743), 6 databases (MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus) were searched from January 1st, 2008 to April 1st, 2026. Data on psychological measures (ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (ACL-RSI), Knee Self-Efficacy Scale (K-SES), Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK)), functional outcomes (International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Limb Symmetry Index (LSI) for knee flexion strength (FLEX-LSI), knee extension strength (EXT-LSI), and single-leg hop distance (SH-LSI)) were extracted from all eligible studies comparing these outcomes between RTS and non-RTS groups, as well as RTPre and non-RTPre groups following primary ACL reconstruction. Effect sizes were pooled as mean differences (continuous variable) or risk ratios (dichotomous variable). Subgroup analyses were stratified by postoperative follow-up time points: ≤6 months, >6-12 months, and >12 months.
RESULTS: A total of 25 studies comprising 7174 patients were included. Overall, the RTS rate was 79.3%, whereas the RTPre rate was 44.1%. The RTPre group exhibited significantly higher ACL-RSI scores than the non-RTPre group, and intergroup difference in ACL-RSI widened progressively over time following ACL reconstruction (≤6 months: mean difference (MD) = 16.09, 95% confidence interval (95%CI): 9.13-23.05; >6-12 months: MD = 18.64, 95%CI: 14.64-22.63; >12 months: MD = 27.07, 95%CI: 22.37-31.76). Similar patterns were observed in the comparison of RTS and non-RTS groups. Compared with the non-RTS group, the RTS group showed higher K-SES scores (MD = 1.27, 95%CI: 1.06-1.87; p < 0.0001) and reduced kinesiophobia (TSK/TSK-11, standardized mean difference (SMD) = -1.15, 95%CI: -2.10 to -0.19, p = 0.02). The RTS group also demonstrated superior functional outcomes vs. the non-RTS group, including IKDC (MD = 7.52, 95%CI: 5.85-9.19), KOOS-Sport/Rec (MD = 11.32, 95%CI: 8.84-13.81), KOOS-quality of life (QoL) (MD = 13.97, 95%CI: 10.83-17.10), EXT-LSI (MD = 7.48%, 95%CI: 2.69-12.26), FLEX-LSI (MD = 3.67%, 95%CI: 0.91-6.43), SH-LSI (MD = 2.96%, 95%CI: 1.77-4.16), though IKDC differences remained below established minimal clinically important difference thresholds.
CONCLUSION: Psychological readiness assessed via the ACL-RSI is important for RTS evaluation after ACL reconstruction. Our analyses uniquely reveal widening between-group gaps in psychological readiness at later recovery stages, with minimal temporal changes in functional differences. Longitudinal monitoring and serial ACL-RSI evaluation across varied postoperative phases is recommended alongside functional assessments to support RTS decision-making.

title: Comparative effectiveness of three splints for rehabilitation after finger flexor tendon repair (FIRST): randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical effectiveness of three splints after repair of zone 1 and 2 flexor tendons: forearm based (long), Manchester short (short), and relative motion flexion (mini) splints.
DESIGN: Prospective, randomised, parallel group, pragmatic, superiority, clinical trial.
SETTING: 26 UK hospitals.
PARTICIPANTS: 430 participants (aged ≥16 years) requiring rehabilitation after primary repair of zone 1 and 2 flexor tendons in one or two fingers of the hand according to British Society for Surgery of the Hand guidelines.
INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1:1 to the long, short, or mini splint. Splints were worn continuously for five weeks and intermittently for a further week at night and in vulnerable situations such as public environments. Masking participants was not possible owing to the nature of the intervention.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the mean post-randomisation score on the patient-rated wrist and hand evaluation (PRWHE) instrument at 6, 12, 26, and 52 weeks, analysed by intention to treat.
RESULTS: 430 participants were randomised to the long splint (n=143), short splint (n=140), or mini splint (n=147) and 403 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. Adherence, defined as wearing the splint for a minimum of five weeks, was 83% (118/143) for the long splint, 76% (106/140) for the short splint, and 78% (115/147) for the mini splint. Mean post-randomisation PRWHE scores were 24.5 (standard deviation 15.5) in the long splint group, 23.5 (16.7) in the short splint group, and 22.4 (15.0) in the mini splint group, with adjusted between group differences of 0.3 (98.3% confidence interval -4.0 to 4.6, P=0.88) for the long versus short splint, 2.3 (-1.9 to 6.5, P=0.19) for the long versus mini splint, and 2.0 (-2.2 to 6.3, P=0.25) for the short versus mini splint. Serious adverse event rates occurred in 10% (14/143) of participants in the long splint group, 11% (15/140) in the short splint group, and 11% (16/147) in the mini splint group.
CONCLUSION: This trial found no statistically significant difference in clinical effectiveness between the long, short, and mini splint. Apart from some small differences, secondary outcomes were comparable across all three groups.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN Registry ISRCTN10236011.

title: Effects and Moderators of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) on Physiological Adaptations Among Team-Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is widely used in team sports, but the influence of participant and programme characteristics on physiological adaptations remains unclear. Five databases (Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CNKI) were searched initially on 25 April 2025 and updated on 21 December 2025. Mixed-effects models were used to estimate Hedges' g and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Forty-six studies involving 1204 athletes were included. Compared with regular sport-specific training alone, HIIT produced positive effects on maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max; g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.61, 0.92]), maximal aerobic power (g = 0.43, 95% CI [0.04, 0.82]), ventilatory threshold (g = 0.70, 95% CI [0.53, 0.88]), Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test performance (g = 1.02, 95% CI [0.76, 1.28]), and 30-s Wingate peak (g = 0.91, 95% CI [0.67, 1.16]) and mean power (g = 0.70, 95% CI [0.39, 1.01]). Effects on body composition were generally unclear. Mutually adjusted multivariable meta-regression identified no convincing evidence of differences in VO2max or Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test performance effects by sex or training level. Longer training duration was associated with greater VO2max effects. In exploratory analyses, model predictions indicated increases in VO2max of 2.56 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI [1.54, 3.58]) after approximately 5 weeks and 5.11 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI [3.32, 6.91]) after approximately 10 weeks. Shorter between-repetition recovery was associated with greater VO2max effects, although other programme variables were estimated imprecisely. Overall, adding HIIT to regular sport-specific training improves aerobic and anaerobic performance in trained team-sport athletes, whereas effects on body composition are limited. Associations involving programme characteristics should be interpreted cautiously because they were derived from study-level meta-regression. Trial Registration: PROSPERO Registration CRD42024609379.

title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain.
PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs.
RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained.
CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

title: Nitric oxide precursor interventions for post-exercise delayed onset muscle soreness: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) commonly follows high-intensity or unaccustomed exercise. Nitric oxide (NO) precursors may reduce DOMS, but their effects remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis to evaluate NO precursor interventions across recovery time points.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched to February 2026 for randomized controlled trials in healthy adults. Interventions were classified into four nodes: beetroot-derived nitrate, watermelon-derived citrulline, synthetic or isolated amino acid precursors (L-arginine and citrulline malate), and watermelon plus added citrulline. Random-effects network meta-analyses were conducted separately at 24, 48, and 72 h. Effects were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); SUCRA rankings were exploratory. Risk of bias and evidence certainty were assessed using RoB 2 and CINeMA, with subgroup and sensitivity analyses examining robustness.
RESULTS: Nineteen trials involving 356 participants were included. At 24 h, watermelon plus added citrulline (SMD = -0.97, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.31) and beetroot-derived nitrate (SMD = -0.67, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.20) significantly reduced DOMS vs. placebo. At 48 h, beetroot-derived nitrate was the only intervention with a significant benefit (SMD = -1.18, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.45). No active intervention differed significantly from placebo at 72 h, while evidence for differences between active interventions was limited, with only watermelon plus added citrulline showing a significant advantage over synthetic or isolated amino acid precursors at 24 h. Beetroot-derived nitrate significantly reduced DOMS vs. placebo in the trained subgroup but not in the untrained subgroup. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the findings, although the beetroot-derived nitrate estimate was sensitive to some restrictions related to the exercise-induced muscle damage model.
CONCLUSION: NO precursor supplementation may reduce post-exercise DOMS at specific recovery time points, particularly with beetroot-derived nitrate and watermelon plus added citrulline. However, evidence for differences between active interventions remains limited, and the sparse network, substantial heterogeneity, and low certainty of evidence preclude firm clinical conclusions.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261373938, identifier: CRD420261373938.

title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels.
METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group.
RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels.
CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Clinical and functional predictors of delayed return to sport after first-time patellar dislocation in adolescents: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: First-time lateral patellar dislocation is common in adolescent athletes and may cause persistent functional impairment despite nonoperative treatment. Early predictors of delayed return to sport remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: To identify early clinical and functional factors associated with delayed return to unrestricted preinjury-level sport after first-time lateral patellar dislocation in adolescents.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 160 adolescents aged 12-18 years (97 females, 63 males) with first-time traumatic lateral patellar dislocation managed nonoperatively. Participants underwent standardized rehabilitation and were followed for 12 months. At 3 months, quadriceps limb-symmetry index (LSI), single-leg hop performance, Y-Balance asymmetry, patellar apprehension, Banff Patellofemoral Instability Instrument 2.0 (BPII 2.0), and Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee scores were assessed. Delayed return to sport was defined as failure to resume unrestricted preinjury-level sport within 6 months. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: Seventy-six participants (47.5%) experienced delayed return to sport. Compared with timely returners, they had lower quadriceps LSI, poorer hop performance, greater Y-Balance asymmetry, more frequent patellar apprehension, and worse patient-reported function. Independent predictors were each 10-percentage-point decrease in quadriceps LSI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.29-2.57), persistent patellar apprehension (aOR 2.71, 95% CI 1.31-5.62), and each 10-point decrease in BPII 2.0 score (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.13-2.02). The model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86).
CONCLUSION: Reduced quadriceps symmetry, persistent apprehension, and poorer instability-specific function were independently associated with delayed return to sport, supporting multidimensional, criterion-based rehabilitation in adolescents.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery after total knee arthroplasty in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture for postoperative pain management and functional recovery in older adults following total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating acupuncture or electroacupuncture for postoperative outcomes in adults undergoing TKA. Primary outcomes included pain intensity (Visual Analogue Scale [VAS]) and functional outcomes (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index [WOMAC], Hospital for Special Surgery [HSS] score, and range of motion). Secondary outcomes included analgesic consumption and adverse events.
RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs involving 1037 participants were included. Acupuncture and electroacupuncture were associated with reduced postoperative pain (VAS: SMD = -1.08, 95% CI, -1.27 to -0.89; Z = 11.09; p < 0.00001) and improved functional outcomes (HSS: SMD = 1.39, 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.75; Z = 7.48; p < 0.00001). No serious adverse events were reported in the included studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Acupuncture may provide beneficial effects on postoperative pain and selected functional outcomes after TKA in older adults. Given the multidisciplinary nature of postoperative recovery, these findings may be relevant to geriatric nursing care, particularly in pain assessment, rehabilitation coordination, and monitoring of recovery. However, the available evidence does not establish acupuncture as a nurse-led intervention.

title: Comparative Effects of Motor-Control Interventions on Neuromuscular and Biomechanical Outcomes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuromuscular-control and biomechanical deficits may persist after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Comparative motor-control effects remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: To compare motor-control interventions after ACLR.
DESIGN: Systematic review and network meta-analysis.
METHOD: Seven databases were searched to 12 May 2026. Usual rehabilitation comprised conventional symptom control, motion, strengthening, gait, or functional training. Three neuromuscular-control outcomes underwent network meta-analysis; k ≥ 2 biomechanical comparisons were pooled and k = 1 estimates unpooled. RoB 2 assessed bias; CINeMA and GRADE assessed confidence.
RESULTS: Thirty-two trials enrolled 1437 participants. Proprioceptive training improved joint position sense versus usual rehabilitation (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.54-1.50; moderate CINeMA confidence); jump-landing control training yielded a favorable dynamic-balance estimate versus usual rehabilitation (1.19, 0.59-1.80; low CINeMA confidence) and was sensitive to exclusion of a late-phase multi-arm athlete trial; feedback-enhanced (0.88, 0.43-1.32) and proprioceptive training (0.59, 0.21-0.97) favored postural control (both low CINeMA confidence). Pooled estimates suggested that neuromuscular training may improve knee valgus and knee flexion kinematics during single-leg landing (1.51, 0.51-2.51; 1.07, 0.49-1.65); pooled gait biomechanical symmetry was inconclusive (-0.41, -0.87-0.05). Across networks, τ² ranged from 0.0275 to 0.1698; global tests detected no statistically clear inconsistency (P = 0.087-0.229), although sparse loop structures limited inference.
CONCLUSION: Moderate-confidence evidence supported proprioceptive training for improving joint position sense after ACLR. Other interventions may help balance and landing control, but their benefits are less certain. The evidence does not establish a single best approach across outcomes.

title: The effect of adding whole-body electromyostimulation to hip and knee strengthening exercises on pain, muscle strength, and function in women with patellofemoral pain syndrome: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Strength training is a key treatment for patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Although conventional strengthening exercises offer important benefits, whole-body electromyostimulation (WB-EMS) may provide complementary advantages; however, its additive effects in PFPS remain unclear.
PURPOSE: This study investigated the short-term effects of adding WB-EMS to hip and knee strengthening exercises on pain and self-reported function in women with PFPS. It also assessed immediate post-treatment effects on muscle strength and objective function.
METHODS: In this single-blind randomized controlled trial, 36 women with unilateral PFPS were randomized to strengthening exercises alone (control) or combined WB-EMS and strengthening exercises (intervention). All performed strengthening exercises three times weekly over 7 weeks (21 sessions); the intervention group additionally received WB-EMS twice weekly (14 sessions). Primary outcomes - worst pain in the previous week (visual analog scale (VAS)) and knee-related symptoms and function (Kujala scale) - were assessed at baseline, 7 weeks, and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes (muscle strength, step-down test repetitions) were measured at baseline and 7 weeks.
RESULTS: Significant group-by-time interactions were found for VAS (F(2,33)=6.41, p = .003, ηp2 = 0.16) and the Kujala scale (F(2,33)=3.86, p = .026, ηp2 = 0.15). VAS was significantly lower in the intervention group at 3 months (mean difference [MD] = -7.64, 95% CI: -9.36 to -3.16, p = .014). Kujala scores were significantly higher at 7 weeks (MD = 5.61, 95% CI: 2.33 to 8.88, p = .001) and 3 months (MD = 7.32, 95% CI: 3.82 to 10.83, p < .001). Significant interactions were also shown for step-down test repetitions (F(1,33)=10.33, p = .003, ηp2 = 0.23), knee extensor strength (F(1,33)=8.06, p = .008, ηp2 = 0.19), and knee flexor strength (F(1,33)=9.21, p = .005, ηp2 = 0.21).
CONCLUSION: Adding WB-EMS to strengthening exercises may improve pain, knee muscle strength, and function in women with unilateral PFPS. Larger, adequately powered trials with appropriate blinding and longer objective follow-up are warranted.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.

title: High Ubiquitin-like Protein 3 Expression Is Associated With Prolonged Recurrence-free Survival in Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Current clinicopathological factors inadequately capture the biological heterogeneity of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This study investigated the prognostic significance of ubiquitin-like protein 3 (UBL3), a molecule involved in extracellular vesicle sorting and immune regulation, in NMIBC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following an exploratory analysis of public RNA-sequencing databases, we evaluated tissue samples from patients who underwent transurethral resection for primary NMIBC. A discovery cohort (n=37) was assessed for UBL3 mRNA via qRT-PCR and protein expression via immunohistochemistry (IHC) quantified using digital H-scores (QuPath). A separate internal validation cohort (n=192) was subsequently evaluated by IHC. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS).
RESULTS: The database analysis indicated that high UBL3 expression was associated with longer RFS in early-stage bladder cancer. In the discovery cohort, higher UBL3 mRNA levels were associated with prolonged RFS [hazard ratio (HR)=0.33, p=0.004]. mRNA levels also were associated with digital H-scores (ρ=0.39, p=0.018). In the separate internal validation cohort, elevated UBL3 protein expression was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence. A multivariable Cox regression confirmed that a higher UBL3 H-score (HR=0.95 per 10-point increase, p=0.023), alongside a negative preoperative urine cytology and immediate intravesical chemotherapy, remained independently associated with RFS.
CONCLUSION: Elevated UBL3 expression was associated with prolonged RFS in patients with NMIBC following transurethral resection of bladder tumor. While UBL3 has potential as a prognostic biomarker, establishing its definitive clinical utility will require mechanistic investigations and validation across independent, multicenter cohorts.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Surgical Profiles of Elite Female Athletes and Their Association with Long-Term Musculoskeletal Health: Findings from the Women's Soccer Health Study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To describe the career and post-career surgeries in female elite-level soccer players and evaluate their association with long-term musculoskeletal health.
STUDY DESIGN: This is a cross-sectional study.
METHODS: Surgical data (the number and type of surgeries during and after the career) from an anonymous online survey was obtained from a previously published cohort of 560 retired elite women's soccer players. Correlation coefficients were used to evaluate the relationship between the number of surgeries and physical activity levels (UCLA activity scale), joint function (SANE), and physical and mental health (PROMIS-10), which were all collected on the same survey.
RESULTS: The average number of career surgeries was 1 (SD=1.6), and the average number of post-career surgeries was 0.5 (SD=1). The most common career surgery sites for women's soccer players were knee (39%), foot/ankle (12%), and leg (4%). The most common knee procedures involved ligament reconstruction, primarily of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), followed by meniscus and cartilage surgery. The most frequent post-career surgery sites were knee (24.0%), foot/ankle (5.1%), and leg (3.2%). Knee ligament and meniscus surgeries were equally reported. More career and post-career surgeries were associated with lower SANE knee scores (p<0.001). Lower SANE knee scores (p=0.017) were associated with lower UCLA activity levels.
CONCLUSIONS: The locations of career and post-career surgeries were similar, suggesting a possible association with long-term musculoskeletal impairment, particularly to the knee, in a cohort of mostly White collegiate former players. Having more soccer-related surgeries was associated with reduced joint function and activity levels after retirement, though the correlations were weak or moderate. These findings suggest the need for the development of preventive interventions that address the specific needs of female athletes, implementation of injury prevention programs and strategies to maximize adherence, and long-term musculoskeletal assessments of players after retirement.

title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology.
RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient.
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

title: Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury initiates biological processes linked to joint tissue degeneration. The longitudinal time course of serum biomarkers reflecting inflammation and cartilage metabolism after ACL reconstruction (ACLR), particularly in comparison with uninjured controls, has not been characterized across the first postoperative year.
HYPOTHESIS: Inflammatory (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 [MCP-1]) and degradative (matrix metalloproteinase-3 [MMP-3]) biomarker concentrations would be elevated pre-ACLR and decrease over time, whereas cartilage turnover biomarker concentrations (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein [COMP] and type II collagen degradation-to-synthesis ratio [C2C:CPII]) would increase postoperatively. Also, pre-ACLR biomarker concentrations would be associated with concentrations at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: A total of 33 individuals with ACL injuries (52% female; mean age, 20.8 ± 2.4 years) were evaluated pre-ACLR and at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. A total of 33 matched uninjured controls were included. Serum concentrations of MCP-1, MMP-3, COMP, and C2C:CPII were assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Linear mixed-effects models with model-based contrasts were used to evaluate differences across groups and time points. ACLR-only linear mixed-effects regression models were used to assess associations between pre-ACLR and follow-up biomarker concentrations. Exploratory post hoc models evaluated differences by concomitant injury status.
RESULTS: MCP-1 was elevated in individuals with ACL injuries compared with controls at all ACLR time points (all Padj < .001), with no change across ACLR time points. MMP-3 increased from pre-ACLR to 6 months post-ACLR (Padj < .001) but did not differ from controls at any time point. COMP was consistently greater in individuals with ACL injuries than in controls at all time points (all Padj≤ .021), with no changes across ACLR time points. C2C:CPII was greater at 12 months post-ACLR than at pre-ACLR and 6 months post-ACLR (both Padj < .001) and than in uninjured controls (Padj = .001). Pre-ACLR MCP-1, MMP-3, and COMP concentrations were associated with concentrations at both 6 and 12 months post-ACLR (all P≤ .006), whereas C2C:CPII was associated only with 12-month concentrations (P = .018).
CONCLUSION: Inflammatory and cartilage-related biomarkers remain altered throughout the first year after ACLR, suggesting that the biological response is not fully resolved by reconstruction and standard rehabilitation but extends beyond the early postoperative period.

title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated.
METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours.
RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones.
CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

title: Recovery of Pre-symptomatic Tegner Activity Level After Double-Level Osteotomy for Medial Compartment Osteoarthritis: Outcomes at 24 Months.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Double-level osteotomy (DLO) provides high return-to-sport rates, but these are generally based on the immediate preoperative activity level, which may already be reduced by knee pain. We evaluated recovery to a recalled pre-symptomatic activity level and associated factors.
HYPOTHESIS: Recovery would be less frequent against the pre-symptomatic reference than the immediate preoperative level.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 51 DLO patients wishing to resume sports, with symptom durations below five years. Tegner activity scale (TAS) scores were recalled for five years before surgery and assessed immediately preoperatively and at 12 and 24 months. Exploratory Firth logistic regression included age, BMI, Kellgren-Lawrence grade, and preoperative Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) to examine failure to recover the five-year TAS at 24 months.
RESULTS: Median [IQR] TAS was 5 [4-8] at the five-year reference, 3 [1-5] preoperatively, 4 [2-5] at 12 months, and 4 [3-7] at 24 months. At 24 months, 56.9% recovered the five-year TAS versus 88.2% recovering the preoperative TAS. Higher PCS was associated with failure to recover the five-year TAS (adjusted OR per point, 1.066; 95% CI, 1.008-1.143; p = 0.025).
DISCUSSION: Recovery proportions differed by reference, with interpretation limited by recall bias and patient selection. Higher PCS was associated with non-recovery in exploratory analysis.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III; retrospective cohort study.

title: Breast Injuries in Women's Rugby Union: A Comparison of Prospective and Retrospective Surveillance.
abstract: Retrospective research has reported a high prevalence of breast injuries in women's rugby union (RU); however, most injuries are not reported to medical staff. This study compared the incidence and severity of breast injuries collected both prospectively and retrospectively over a comparable match exposure period. Prospective surveillance was conducted by clinicians (n = 14) using an online injury surveillance system across 140 RU players. Retrospective surveillance was conducted using an anonymous online survey completed by 370 RU players. Injury incidence was calculated per 1000 hours of match exposure. Severity was assessed using breast pain, bruising and swelling, ability to continue play, perceived effect on performance, and long-term breast changes. Three breast injuries were prospectively recorded over 1204 hours of competition (2.5 injuries/1000 hours). In contrast, 144 breast injuries were reported retrospectively over 5055 hours of competition (28.5 injuries/1000 hours). The retrospective injury rate was significantly higher than the prospective rate (IRR = 11.4, 95% CI: 3.15-41.73; p < 0.002). Ninety-six percent (n = 139) of retrospectively reported injuries had not been disclosed to medical staff. Injury severity was similar between surveillance methods, with bruising commonly reported, all players continuing to participate despite injury, and over half perceiving a negative effect on performance. Long-term breast changes were reported by 6% (n = 8) of players. The substantially lower incidence recorded prospectively suggests that breast injuries are underreported in women's RU. Improved reporting and surveillance strategies are required to better capture breast injuries and support female athlete health and performance.

title: Baseline Performance and the 72-Hour Performance Window Following Plyometric Withdrawal in Collegiate Sprinters.
abstract: Plyometric studies emphasise pre-post change, but coaches need to know what remains after the block ends. This single-cohort study followed 26 collegiate sprinters through 12 weeks of Monday plyometric training and 4 weeks of withdrawal, without a parallel control group. During intervention, 30 m sprint time and arm-assisted countermovement jump (CMJ) height were measured at 0, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h; 0 and 72 h were retained during withdrawal. Mixed models showed large week effects for sprint, F(1, 1534) = 2272.01, partial η2 = 0.597, 95% CI [0.570, 0.622], and CMJ, F(1, 1534) = 2537.82, partial η2 = 0.623, 95% CI [0.598, 0.647]. Time-point effects were evident, but week × time-point interactions were not. Relative to 0 h, sprint was 0.0098 s slower at 24 h and 0.0057 s faster at 72 h; CMJ was 0.311 cm lower at 24 h and 0.245 cm higher at 72 h (all Tukey-adjusted p < 0.001). Linear, quadratic, and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models were compared by rolling one-step error. ARIMA had the lowest rolling errors and provided exploratory, model-based references for weeks 13-16. During withdrawal, 1/4 sprint and 0/4 CMJ 0 h observations fell within the 95% prediction interval; mean absolute deviations were 0.0233 s and 0.794 cm. Three of four 72 - 0 h observations were within the interval for both outcomes. The 72 - 0 h series more often fell within their model-based intervals than the 0 h series, indicating different short-term patterns.

title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs).
METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests.
RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

title: TAICHIKNEE trial: protocol for an embedded pragmatic, individually randomised group-treatment trial of remotely delivered Tai Chi for knee osteoarthritis across US healthcare systems.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of chronic pain and disability and is associated with substantial healthcare utilisation and costs. In-person Tai Chi, a multidimensional mind-body exercise, is recommended as a non-pharmacological therapy for knee OA; however, delivery through in-person classes may limit scalability across US healthcare systems. Remote delivery may reduce logistical barriers and facilitate integration into routine care, but evidence regarding its effectiveness and implementation in real-world healthcare settings remains limited. We describe the protocol for TAICHIKNEE, an embedded pragmatic trial evaluating remotely delivered group Tai Chi plus routine care vs routine care alone for adults with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: TAICHIKNEE is a 12-month, fully decentralised, embedded pragmatic, individually randomised group-treatment trial with an effectiveness-implementation hybrid type 1 design conducted across five US healthcare systems. The trial will randomise 480 adults aged ≥50 years with symptomatic, clinician-diagnosed knee OA in a 1:1 ratio within six sequential cohorts, stratified by healthcare system and sex. Participants assigned to Tai Chi will receive 24 live, instructor-led 60-minute videoconference sessions over 12 weeks in addition to routine care; control participants will continue routine care. The cohort randomisation date defines time zero for both groups. The primary outcome is Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) pain at 3 months, analysed using a partially nested mixed-effects model that accounts for clustering within Tai Chi classes and adjusts for baseline WOMAC pain and prespecified covariates. Key secondary outcomes are Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Pain Interference and SF-12 health-related quality of life scores at 3 months, and knee joint injections over 12 months. Safety will be assessed throughout the 12-month follow-up. The implementation evaluation will concurrently assess intervention fidelity, stakeholder perspectives and participant and instructor experiences using Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research-informed stakeholder interviews, fidelity assessments and surveys to identify factors influencing implementation and inform future sustainment and spread across healthcare systems.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval was obtained from the Tufts University Health Sciences Institutional Review Board (IRB) (STUDY00003780), serving as the single IRB of record for all participating sites. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences and stakeholder engagement activities across healthcare systems. De-identified participant-level data and study materials will be shared in accordance with applicable data-sharing policies, participant consent, IRB requirements and the approved data-sharing plan.

title: Test-Retest Reliability of Soft Tissue Vibration Variables Across an Outdoor 5-km Run.
abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the test-retest reliability of soft tissue vibration (STV) measurements taken superficial to the medial gastrocnemius during a 5-km outdoor run. Twenty-eight trained athlete participants (female: n = 14 and male: n = 14) wore a triaxial inertial measurement unit mounted on the skin superficial to their medial gastrocnemius (500 Hz) and performed two 5-km outdoor runs on different days at a controlled, individualized pace. STV outcome measures-peak acceleration, damping coefficient, settling time, peak and median frequency, and power-were analyzed using a continuous wavelet transform from averaged running strides within the entire run and among three 1500-m segments from each testing session. Intraclass correlation coefficients reinforced good to excellent between-day reliability measures (.75-.92) for all STV outcome measures except peak frequency (.50) and moderate to excellent reliability when comparing days across the 3 segments of the run (.70-.94), except for peak frequency (.44-.57). No significant day × time interactions were observed (P = .06-.63). Overall, STV outcome measures assessed with an inertial measurement unit during outdoor running demonstrated good reliability, supporting methodologies to quantify STV in real-world settings with potential applications in running performance and injury prevention research.

title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Blood Flow Restriction in Upper-Extremity Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review of Clinical Studies.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of blood flow restriction (BFR) therapy on upper-extremity strength, pain, range of motion, and functional outcomes.
METHODS: This systematic review followed the 2009 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from January 2000 through August 2025 for studies evaluating upper-extremity BFR during resistance or therapeutic exercise. Studies were included if they were randomized controlled trials or prospective studies published in English that reported pre- and postintervention outcomes of strength, pain, range of motion, muscle morphology, or validated functional scores.
RESULTS: A total of 492 studies were identified, 5 of which met inclusion criteria, encompassing 128 participants. Four studies (80%) were randomized controlled trials, and 1 study (20%) was a prospective cohort study. Clinical indications for the use of BFR included rotator cuff tendinopathy, lateral epicondylitis, distal radius fracture rehabilitation, and postoperative shoulder rehabilitation. Four of 5 studies (80%) showed statistically significant BFR-related improvements in strength, with the remaining study reporting within-group improvements that did not reach between-group significance. Three of 4 studies (75%) that assessed pain reported significant reductions favoring BFR, with the fourth showing clinically within-group pain reductions in both BFR and control. Notable findings included a significant between-group improvement in internal rotation strength at 60°/s favoring BFR in rotator cuff tendinopathy (P = .04) and significant pain reduction in distal radius fracture rehabilitation (visual analog scale: 5.5 → 1.5, P = .03).
CONCLUSIONS: In this systematic review, 4 of 5 studies (80%) reported statistically significant strength improvements favoring BFR, and 3 of 4 studies (75%) assessing pain showed significant reductions favoring BFR, with no serious adverse events reported. These findings support BFR as a promising adjunct in upper-extremity rehabilitation; however, heterogeneity in study design and intervention parameters limits definitive conclusions.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level I and IV studies.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43465-026-01939-3.

title: Patients Undergoing Proximal Hamstring Repair Have High Rates of Return to Work and Favorable Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate return-to-work (RTW) rates and functional outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring tendon avulsion injuries.
METHODS: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus were searched in April 2025 for studies reporting RTW outcomes after surgical repair of proximal hamstring avulsions. Eligible studies involved human subjects undergoing open or endoscopic repair and reporting RTW rates or patient counts. No minimum follow-up duration was required. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, with discrepancies resolved by a third. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies criteria.
RESULTS: Six studies (229 patients) met inclusion criteria. Four studies reported an overall RTW rate ranging from 89% to 100%, whereas 2 studies stratified outcomes by Workers' Compensation (WC) status, showing lower RTW rates among WC patients (70.0%-86.3%) compared with non-WC patients (92.5%-94.1%). Return-to-sport rates, when reported, ranged from 58% to 100%. Study-level RTW and return-to-sport outcomes were summarized descriptively without pooled estimates because of heterogeneity in study design, surgical approach, injury chronicity, WC status, and outcome definitions. Complication rates were low overall, with retear or reoperation occurring in 0% to 5.8% of cases. Clinically relevant patient improvement thresholds were only reported in 1 study.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study, most patients undergoing surgical repair for proximal hamstring avulsion injuries return to work with favorable functional outcomes and low complication rates.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level III and IV studies.
