title: Effects of Integrative Neuromuscular Training on Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Extremity Sports Performance in Adolescent Female Sprinters: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent female athletes often exhibit more pronounced lower-limb asymmetry due to physiological differences, increasing injury risk. Despite documented efficacy in team sports for injury mitigation and performance enhancement, integrative neuromuscular training (INT) effects on unilateral and bilateral lower-limb capabilities in trained adolescent female sprinters remain undetermined.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that an 8-week INT program would significantly improve unilateral and bilateral lower-extremity performance measures in adolescent female sprinters compared with traditional sprint-specific training.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Twenty-four national second-level adolescent female sprinters (aged 16-18 years) were randomly assigned to an 8-week INT group (n = 12) or a control group (CON, n = 12) that continued traditional sprint-specific training. Measurements obtained before and after the intervention included the hop test, star excursion balance test (SEBT), 3-repetition maximum (3RM) unilateral and bilateral back squat, 100-m run, standing long jump (SLJ), and limb symmetry index (LSI).
RESULTS: After the intervention, the INT group outperformed the CON group on the nondominant side in all hop tests (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.74-0.88), six directions of the SEBT (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.44-0.88), and the 3RM unilateral back squat (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.65). On the dominant side, the INT group also outperformed the CON group in the single hop for distance (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.80) and three directions of the SEBT (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.38-0.84). In addition, the INT group showed significantly greater improvements than the CON group in the LSI from unilateral tests (all P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.26-0.88), as well as in the 100-m run and SLJ (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.61-0.69).
CONCLUSION: The 8-week INT program was associated with improvements in dynamic balance, explosive power, and limb symmetry in adolescent female sprinters, with greater benefits observed on the nondominant side.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: INT is an effective training modality for improving lower-limb performance and mitigating asymmetry in adolescent female sprinters.

title: Acute and Chronic Effects of Parachute-Resisted Sprint Training on Sprint Performance and Sprint Mechanics: A Systematic Review with GRADE Assessment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Parachute-resisted sprint training (PRST) is a practical field-based resisted-sprint method that uses aerodynamic drag to provide sprint-specific overload. Although PRST has been widely used in athletic settings, evidence on its acute mechanical effects and chronic training adaptations remains heterogeneous.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to synthesize the acute and chronic effects of PRST on sprint performance, sprint mechanics, neuromuscular responses, and sprint-related physiological outcomes in healthy, physically active, and athletic populations.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus on 17th May 2026. Original empirical studies were eligible if they examined PRST or parachute-resisted sprinting and reported outcomes related to sprint performance, biomechanics, neuromuscular responses, or sprint-related physiology. Studies were synthesized narratively and grouped into acute and chronic evidence streams. Methodological quality was assessed using the Modified Downs and Black checklist, and certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies were included (8 acute and 9 chronic). In acute comparisons, PRST consistently reduced sprint velocity or increased sprint time; where directly reported, velocity reductions were approximately 3.4-6% relative to unresisted sprinting. Larger parachute conditions generally produced greater velocity decrements and changes in horizontal force or impulse variables. Chronic studies reported improvements in selected sprint outcomes, including 0-10 m, 10-20 m, and 0-20 m splits in one randomized study; other studies reported improvements such as 3.48% in 60-yd performance and 0.618 s in 100-m performance. However, chronic studies' findings were heterogeneous, and evidence for maximal velocity, neuromuscular or energetic outcomes, and population-specific effects remained limited.
CONCLUSIONS: PRST appears to provide a practical, sprint-specific overload and may improve selected sprint performance outcomes. However, the current evidence base is limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous protocols, poor quantification of resistance, inconsistent reporting of outcomes, and limited comparator control. Based on GRADE, confidence in the evidence is generally 'low' to 'very low' across most outcomes. Trial Registration (OSF) https://osf.io/56nct DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/8SJW4.

title: Creatine supplementation in soccer players: a systematic review.
abstract:
AIM: Soccer places repeated demands on short-duration, high-intensity performance, including sprints, accelerations, jumps, and technical actions performed over the course of a match. Because these efforts depend heavily on rapid adenosine triphosphate (ATP) resynthesis, creatine is a plausible ergogenic aid for soccer players. However, findings in soccer-specific studies have been inconsistent, and previous reviews have addressed narrower questions using smaller evidence sets. This systematic review therefore examined the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes in soccer players.
METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 15 May 2025 in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. We included controlled clinical trials of creatine supplementation in male or female soccer players of any age or competitive level when an eligible placebo, control, or comparison condition was available. Outcomes were grouped into performance, body composition, and recovery/fatigue domains. Domains from the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool were used to produce study-level methodological summaries rather than formal result-specific risk-of-bias assessments. Because the studies differed substantially in design, supplementation protocols, populations, and outcomes, findings were synthesised qualitatively rather than pooled in a meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Source-level verification left 45 eligible reports representing 41 unique studies: 28 randomised parallel-group studies, 2 randomised crossover/repeated-condition studies, and 11 non-randomised or allocation-unverifiable controlled studies. Some trials reported favourable findings for repeated-sprint performance, anaerobic power, and muscular strength, but the comparative evidence was inconsistent and the certainty of evidence was very low. Findings for vertical jump performance and technical skills were mixed, while change-of-direction and endurance outcomes showed no consistent benefit. Recovery- and fatigue-related findings were also largely null or inconsistent. Body mass often increased, particularly after loading protocols, whereas evidence for gains in lean mass was limited and inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: The soccer-specific evidence for creatine supplementation remains suggestive rather than conclusive. Favourable findings have been reported for some repeated-sprint, anaerobic-power, and strength outcomes, but the comparative evidence is heterogeneous, often limited by unclear or nonsignificant between-group effects, and of very low certainty. Firm conclusions about efficacy are therefore not possible. Body mass commonly increased, especially after loading protocols, while effects on lean mass, endurance, change-of-direction ability, and recovery/fatigue-related outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: Orthobiologics in Focus: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions, A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Regenerative modalities are increasingly becoming part of orthopedic practice with the use of orthobiologic interventions. These interventions make use of biological approaches to help in repairing the tissues, mitigating nociception, and improving locomotor performance.
OBJECTIVE: The current scoping review is a review of the modern literature as of 2020-2025 on orthobiologic therapies. It examines their clinical effectiveness, the strength of supporting evidence, and the development of new progress in musculoskeletal pathology regenerative management.
METHODS: A systematic search in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and WoS was done on the articles with their indexes dated between January 2020 and February 2025. The inclusion criteria were human and animal studies that utilized platelet-rich plasma (PRP), (MSCs), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), and adipose-derived products strategies using a scaffold only. Synthesis and data extraction were conducted as per PRISMA-ScR standards.
RESULTS: Among the 1716 records that had been filtered, 81 studies met inclusion criteria. Most of them were randomized or comparative trials (77% Level I-II evidence), which are evidence of the high methodological quality. PRP was the most commonly researched modality, whereas MSC-based interventions were the most common.
CONCLUSION: PRP, MSCs, and BMAC are orthobiologic modalities, which are evidence-based and effective alternatives to promote musculoskeletal healing and regeneration. These interventions supplemented by conventional surgical procedures and rehabilitative interventions yield pain relief, functional restoration, and long-term joint maintenance in a spectrum of orthopedic complications.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

title: A Narrative Review of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Graft Choice and Its Influence on Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most common knee injuries in active individuals and can lead to persistent instability, secondary intra-articular damage, and an elevated risk of osteoarthritis. Because return to sport (RTS) is a major goal for most active patients and graft selection remains one of the most debated aspects of ACL reconstruction, this narrative review summarizes the contemporary evidence on how graft choice influences RTS, focusing on the four most common grafts: bone-patellar tendon-bone (BTB), hamstring tendon (HT), quadriceps tendon (QT), and allograft.
RECENT FINDINGS: RTS rates range from ~ 65% to 73% at three years and are higher (83-90%) in elite and high-school athletes. In young, active patients, autografts are associated with higher RTS and lower revision rates than allografts, and high-level evidence-including randomized-trial meta-analyses-has not established the superiority of any single autograft. BTB offers reliable bone-to-bone healing and low revision rates; HT reduces donor-site morbidity and anterior knee pain but has variable diameter and possible flexion weakness; and QT is a versatile option with favorable biomechanics, low donor-site morbidity, and encouraging RTS data, including in skeletally immature athletes. RTS is one of several important outcomes after ACL reconstruction, alongside long-term joint health and reinjury prevention. For RTS, the literature supports autograft over allograft in young, active patients while identifying no universally superior autograft. Graft selection should be individualized to patient age, sport, activity level, anatomy, and reinjury risk; the senior author favors QT or BTB autografts for high-demand athletes.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Quadriceps Strength After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Mechanisms of Weakness and Evidence-Based Rehabilitation Strategies.
abstract: Impairment of quadriceps strength is a frequent and clinically important problem after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and reconstruction. This dysfunction reflects muscular, neural, surgical, and rehabilitation-related mechanisms and is not solely attributable to muscle atrophy. Despite restoration of joint stability, quadriceps weakness can persist and contribute to delayed functional recovery and reduced readiness to return to sport. A comprehensive assessment should integrate clinical examination, objective isometric or isokinetic strength testing, rate of force development, functional performance, quality of movement, imaging investigations, and patient-reported and psychological measures. Rehabilitation should be initiated preoperatively and continue postoperatively with a focus on control of effusion and restoration of extension, early quadriceps activation, progressive resistance exercise, appropriate open-chain loading followed by eccentric, plyometric, and sport-specific training. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation has supportive evidence as an adjunct, and blood-flow restriction training may be useful when higher loads may not yet be tolerated. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the mechanisms and rehabilitation of quadriceps weakness after ACL injury and ACL reconstruction, highlighting clinically relevant strategies for restoring strength and neuromuscular function.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Editorial Commentary: Allograft Reconstruction in Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tendon Avulsions: Bridging the Gap May Not Equal a Full Return.
abstract: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsions are being treated surgically at rising rates, and although primary repair reliably restores function and return to sport in the acute setting, chronic and significantly retracted tears present a far more difficult problem. When direct repair is not feasible for a chronic, retracted proximal hamstring tendon avulsion, allograft reconstruction offers a bridge across a gap that would otherwise go unaddressed. However, significant chronicity and retraction are difficult challenges to overcome, and patient expectations must be appropriately counseled. As a salvage procedure, allograft reconstruction may improve patient outcomes significantly; however, it is not expected to restore full function, return athletic individuals to their baseline and preinjury level of sports participation, or match the success of primary repair. Allograft reconstruction may also carry more than double the risk of rerupture, which is important to discuss with patients up front. Graft choice and postoperative rehabilitation protocols remain heterogeneous across the limited available literature, and a validated tool to risk-stratify which chronic, retracted tears are best served by reconstruction versus continued nonoperative management does not yet exist. These findings suggest that allograft reconstruction is a viable and clinically meaningful option for a difficult, often nonoperatively unsalvageable problem, but surgeons should frame it for patients as a salvage procedure rather than a full restoration of function, and expectations should be set accordingly.

title: Multi-Modal Biometric Fusion for Athletic Performance Optimization: Clinical Validation of the Dynamic Multi-Sensor Fusion Classifier (DMSFC).
abstract: Integrating real-time biometric monitoring into sports science is increasingly important for optimizing athletic performance and reducing injury risk. However, many existing systems have limited capacity to accurately combine data from multiple biometric sources. This study evaluated the Dynamic Multisensor Fusion (DMSFC) classifier for analyzing physiological and functional data collected from multiple biometric modalities, including electrocardiography (ECG), fingerprint measurements, and facial recognition. A multimodal biometric framework based on DMSFC was developed to monitor and classify key health and performance indicators in elite athletes. The variables evaluated included heart rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure (BP), flexibility, muscle strength, and endurance capacity. The performance of the classifier was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). After implementing the proposed monitoring framework, improvements were observed in the evaluated performance and health indicators. The mean heart rate decreased from 78 to 66 beats per minute, while oxygen saturation slightly increased from 98% to 99%. Blood pressure decreased from 120/80 mmHg to 110/70 mmHg. Flexibility improved from 32 to 36 cm, muscle strength increased from 105 to 122 pounds, and endurance capacity increased from 20 to 24 minutes. Among the evaluated classifiers, DMSFC showed a strongest overall performance (i.e., accuracy of 0.94, sensitivity of 0.91, specificity of 0.96, and AUC of 0.97). These findings suggest that DMSFC could be capable of providing an effective framework for multimodal biometric analysis in sports science. Its use may support athlete assessment, facilitate the development of individualized training programs, and contribute to injury prevention strategies. Because the reported physiological changes were observed after implementation of the framework, further controlled studies are needed to determine whether they were caused by the monitoring system, the associated exercise program, or other factors.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Exostosis of the sustentaculum tali causing tibiotarsal joint pathology in a Standardbred racehorse trotter.
abstract: This report describes a novel case of exostosis on the medial aspect of the sustentaculum tali, (ST) associated with tibiotarsal joint (TTJ) pathology, without involvement of the tarsal sheath or lateral digital flexor tendon. A 5-year-old Standardbred gelding was presented with right TTJ effusion and exercise-induced hind-limb lameness. Diagnostic imaging identified a columnar periosteal proliferation on the medial ST, accompanied by synovial effusion and joint capsule thickening; however, the tarsal sheath and lateral digital flexor tendon remained unremarkable. Although TTJ arthroscopy confirmed synovitis, it did not allow visualization of the exostosis. The lesion was successfully excised via an ultrasound-guided extra-articular surgical approach. Postoperative management included a structured rehabilitation program, resulting in a return to full-speed training by Day 76 with no recurrence of lameness. Follow-up evaluations demonstrated improved performance and complete resolution of TTJ effusion and associated swelling. This case highlighted the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying extra-synovial lesions of the ST and supported ultrasound-guided extra-articular removal as an effective surgical option for ST exostosis. Although the underlying cause of the lesion was uncertain, subclinical trauma was considered a likely contributing factor. Key clinical message: The ST is a horizontal bony projection on the plantaromedial aspect of the calcaneus. Due to its minimal soft-tissue coverage, it is particularly vulnerable to external trauma and subsequent osseous proliferation. Exostosis of the ST may result in impingement of the plantaromedial pouch of the tarsocrural (tibiotarsal) joint, contributing to joint irritation and secondary pathology. Accurate diagnosis and effective case management rely on the combined use of radiography and ultrasonography, which together enable detailed assessment of both osseous changes and associated soft-tissue structures.

title: Immediate effect of verbal cues on ACL injury relevant Knee loading during 180° and 90° cutting maneuvers in female university soccer and basketball athletes.
abstract: Young female athletes possess a high risk of rupturing their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). High external peak knee abduction moments (pKAM) are a likely key risk factor for non-contact ACL injuries. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of performance-based movement feedback on pKAM during cutting maneuvers in female university athletes. Thirty-four female university soccer and basketball athletes completed preplanned 180° and 90° cutting trials while ground reaction forces and kinematics were simultaneously captured. Participants immediately received verbal cues targeting foot strike angle, foot progression angle, or trunk lean angle based on their performance. Athletes then repeated the trials post-feedback. Changes in pKAM between baseline and post-feedback trials were analyzed. Soccer and basketball athletes who received the FOOTstrike-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM for both cutting tasks (Soccer: 180°; -0.21 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.92; 90°; -0.28 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 1.16. Basketball: 180°; -0.07 Nm/kg, p = 0.02, d = 0.76; 90°; -0.30 Nm/kg, p < 0.01, d = 0.82). The FOOTpro-angle cue significantly reduced pKAM during the 180° cut for soccer athletes (-0.10 Nm/kg, p = 0.01, d = 0.60), but not basketball. The TRUNKlean cue did not significantly affect pKAM for either sport. Individual feedback targeting forefoot landings and neutral foot progression angles can elicit immediate technique change and reduce ACL injury relevant knee loading during cutting maneuvers.

title: Facilitators and Barriers to Treatment Access and Use in Black Individuals With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Qualitative Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury are at high risk of knee osteoarthritis. Black individuals with osteoarthritis have worse pain and disability than White individuals. Racial disparities in ACL treatment use (ACL reconstruction and physical therapy) may contribute to disparities in long-term osteoarthritis-related disability. However, factors influencing ACL injury disparities are unknown. We explored facilitators and barriers to treatment access and use in Black individuals with ACL injury.
DESIGN: Qualitative (semistructured interviews).
METHODS: We included Black or African American individuals who self-reported ACL injury up to 5 years prior to recruitment, no longer seeking care for the injury, and 16-50 years old. We conducted one-on-one semistructured interviews and topics included facilitators and barriers to care, perceived communication, medical trust, and perceived discrimination. We used a reflexive thematic analysis approach to analyze the interviews.
RESULTS: We included 10 participants (age 21-49 y, 8 women). We generated 4 themes: (1) path to diagnosis, (2) patient approach to treatment, (3) patient-provider interactions, and (4) life demands. ACL injury recovery was often complex with frustrations particularly common during the diagnosis process due to lack of an accurate diagnosis and poor communication on next steps. Participants took various approaches to treatment use including active, passive, and more autonomous approaches. Family obligations and transportation barriers posed challenges to accessing treatment. Lack of health insurance was a barrier affecting multiple aspects of recovery. Participants often desired shared decision making. Several types of perceived discrimination were discussed including race, gender, insurance, and weight. Facilitators were often related to positive communication or athletic program resources.
CONCLUSION: Facilitators included shared decision making, provider empathy and encouragement, and athletic program resources. Barriers included a lack of listening to patients' concerns, lack of health insurance, transportation challenges, and perceived discrimination.

title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
abstract: Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: Weightbearing CT in the Evaluation of Athletic Foot and Ankle Injuries.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Subtle foot and ankle injuries in athletes, including syndesmotic sprains, ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures, may be underestimated or misclassified on conventional imaging. This review summarizes the current role of weightbearing CT (WBCT) in their evaluation, focusing on quantitative parameters, recent technical advances, and their potential influence on clinical decision-making.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent evidence has shifted WBCT from qualitative assessment toward reproducible three-dimensional quantification. Volumetric assessment and distance mapping improve characterization of syndesmotic instability, while external-rotation stress can reveal abnormalities not evident during neutral standing. In the midfoot, triplanar realignment and side-to-side comparison improve the reliability of Lisfranc measurements and support detection of subtle instability. Distance mapping permits reproducible quantification of osteochondral lesion surface area, depth, and volume and may improve consistency in surgical planning. WBCT has also characterized sport-specific alignment patterns and a morphologic and bone-density phenotype associated with proximal fifth metatarsal stress fractures. Semiautomated segmentation and deep-learning methods may further reduce observer dependence and analysis time. WBCT provides three-dimensional measurements under physiologic load that complement clinical examination and conventional imaging in selected athletic foot and ankle conditions. Its greatest current value lies in characterizing subtle instability, malalignment, and osseous morphology when these findings may alter treatment planning. However, most available evidence is retrospective and derived from symptomatic or injured cohorts. Prospective studies are needed to validate diagnostic thresholds, determine whether WBCT-derived parameters predict injury or outcomes, and define their role in routine athletic screening and return-to-sport decision-making.

title: The Role of Physical Preparation in Motorsport Athletes Across Different Vehicle Types: A Narrative Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite motorsport's widespread appeal, early performance models did not consider drivers as athletes, and even drivers often struggled with this classification, which historically contributed to their exclusion from research focused on athletic performance. Slowly but steadily, this paradigm has been changing.
PURPOSE: To review the evolution of physical conditioning in land-based motorsports and to examine the specific physiological and physical demands imposed on drivers by different vehicle types. A narrative review was conducted to synthesize historical perspectives, physiological demands, and training approaches in motorsport. Peer-reviewed studies, practical reports, opinion articles, and relevant online materials were analyzed to describe the evolution of the physical conditioning required across racing categories. The physical demands in motorsports are characterized by sustained cardiovascular strain, significant neuromuscular loading, large and sustained G-force exposure, and pronounced thermal stress. These demands vary according to vehicle type. Closed-wheel drivers are particularly exposed to prolonged heat stress and require comprehensive muscular endurance and thermoregulatory adaptation. Open-wheel drivers experience large G-forces, demanding exceptional neck and lower-limb strength. Two-wheel riders require enhanced handgrip strength, dynamic neuromuscular control, and high levels of aerobic capacity.
CONCLUSIONS: Tailored conditioning programs addressing the distinct physiological, neuromuscular, and thermoregulatory demands of each motorsport category are closely linked to performance and safety. Further systematic evaluation of the empirical evidence is necessary to enhance the ecological validity of training recommendations and strengthen their application in competitive motorsport.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: The gut-muscle-joint axis in osteoarthritis: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Emerging evidence highlights a complex crosstalk between the gut microbiota, musculoskeletal tissues, and the joint microenvironment, revealing osteoarthritis (OA) as a systemic disorder rather than a localized cartilage disease. The gut-muscle-joint interaction integrates microbial dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation to influence cartilage homeostasis, muscle strength, and neuromuscular stability. Building upon previously described gut-osteoarthritis and gut-muscle interactions, the Gut-Muscle-Joint (GMJ) axis is presented as an integrative framework linking intestinal permeability, microbial metabolites, systemic inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular health, skeletal muscle function, and joint integrity. Perturbations in this axis amplify oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix degradation across musculoskeletal tissues. Understanding GMJ axis-driven mechanisms offers novel preventive and therapeutic strategies that target microbiome restoration, metabolic reprogramming, and neuromuscular health through probiotics, postbiotics, AMPK-SIRT1 activators, and structured exercise. This integrative perspective positions the GMJ axis as a unifying framework for intervention, enabling precision approaches to preserve joint function, reduce sarcopenia, and attenuate OA progression.

title: Rethinking early arthrogenic muscle inhibition after total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: We read with interest the recent article by Barrera Uso et al. on early arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The study provides clinically relevant evidence that AMI at 30 days strongly predicts persistence at 60 days. We suggest, however, that this finding should be interpreted as a prognostic association rather than evidence that 30-day AMI is the dominant biological determinant of subsequent inhibition. We also discuss the timing of postoperative assessment, noting that evaluation at 30 days is appropriate for studying persistence but less informative regarding the initial pathophysiological development of AMI. The Scientific Anterior Cruciate Ligament Network International (SANTI) classification has demonstrated excellent reliability in anterior cruciate ligament populations, although its generalizability to TKA remains to be specifically established. Finally, the absence of objective functional and patient-reported outcomes limits interpretation of the clinical significance of persistent AMI. Overall, the study identifies an important clinical phenotype and useful prognostic markers while leaving the underlying mechanisms of persistence to be further clarified.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Fluoroscopy-Guided Intra-Articular Hip Corticosteroid Injections: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Utility, Technique, and Steroid Selection.
abstract: Intra-articular hip corticosteroid injection is a practical option for selected patients with hip pain, particularly osteoarthritis, and may also clarify whether symptoms arise from the hip rather than the lumbar spine or periarticular structures. This review evaluates the diagnostic and therapeutic utility of injections performed under fluoroscopy, summarizes technique, and discusses steroid selection and dosing. # Recent Findings Randomized trials and contemporary syntheses support clinically meaningful short-term improvement in pain and function after image-guided hip corticosteroid injection, although durability is variable and repeated-injection data remain limited. Fluoroscopy provides continuous visualization of osseous landmarks and contrast-confirmed intra-articular spread. Ultrasound avoids radiation and may be more convenient depending on physician comfort level and ultrasound skills. Safety discussions have emphasized transient systemic effects, uncertain associations with rapidly progressive osteoarthritis, and the timing of injection before arthroplasty. # Summary Fluoroscopy-guided injection remains a reliable, reproducible diagnostic and therapeutic tool when the pain generator is uncertain or short-term symptom control may facilitate rehabilitation, bridge care, or support shared surgical decision-making. Benefit depends on careful patient selection, technically confirmed intra-articular delivery, conservative dosing, and explicit counseling that relief is usually temporary and that structural disease is not reversed.

title: Is the annular ligament disrupted in Monteggia fracture-dislocations? A cadaveric mechanistic study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is characterized by an ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation. The mechanisms of dislocation and annular ligament integrity remain unclear. This study established a cadaveric Monteggia fracture-dislocation model to investigate radial head dislocation and associated annular ligament injury.
METHODS: Twelve upper limbs from 6 fresh-frozen cadavers (mean age at death, 83 years; 1 male, 5 females) were examined. Soft tissues were removed while preserving the bones, ligaments, capsules, forearm interosseous membrane, and biceps tendon insertions. The humeroulnar joint was fixed at 90° flexion, and the ulna was manually fractured to create a Bado type I (direct-blow) Monteggia fracture-dislocation model. The annular ligament, quadrate ligament, oblique cord (Weitbrecht ligament), and forearm interosseous membrane were evaluated.
RESULTS: Ulnar fracture created forearm deformity, causing the radius to contact the triangular fulcrum. Continued manual loading caused the radius to pivot around the fulcrum. The annular ligament remained intact in 11 of 12 limbs; 1 specimen showed injury at the annular ligament-capsular junction. In 11 limbs, the radial head was dislocated beneath the distal margin of the annular ligament. One quadrate ligament rupture occurred; the oblique cord and forearm interosseous membrane remained intact.
CONCLUSION: In this standardized cadaveric direct-blow model, anterior radial head dislocation occurred in 11 of 12 limbs, beneath the distal margin of an intact annular ligament. These findings demonstrate that annular ligament rupture is not required for radial head dislocation in the described experimental setting. This mechanism provides a possible anatomic explanation for difficult reduction in selected cases.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.
